analysis.one_liner: Loosens clean air rules for oil refineries and subsidizes new refinery and pipeline construction.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 212-210 on October 7, 2005 with zero Democratic votes, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Written in the weeks after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita disrupted Gulf Coast refining, the bill tried to spur new refinery construction by designating federal land — including closed military bases — for refineries, putting the Energy Department in charge of permitting with court-enforced deadlines, and paying companies that built new refineries for delays caused by lawsuits or agency inaction. It also loosened Clean Air Act rules, let the President temporarily waive fuel requirements during disasters, and streamlined pipeline siting. Alongside those industry measures it included an FTC ban on price gouging in disaster areas and small carpool grants. The House passed it 212-210 on a strictly party-line vote; the Senate committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil refiners and pipeline developers gain the most: federal backup payments covering delay costs including debt interest, presidentially designated refinery sites on federal land, a single lead agency with deadlines that agencies must meet, and review of challenges consolidated in one federal appeals court. Small refineries gain rebates on federal royalty oil. Drivers benefit only indirectly and hypothetically, through the bill's stated goal of more fuel supply, plus a narrow FTC price-gouging ban during disasters and modest carpool grants.

how_it_helps.text: The Energy Secretary can contract with the first companies to commit to building or reopening refineries and pay them all costs of delays caused by litigation or agency inaction — including interest on their debt and consequential damages — from a federal Standby Refinery Support Account.

The Department of Energy becomes the lead agency coordinating all federal refinery approvals, other agencies must comply with its deadlines, and all legal challenges go to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals on an expedited schedule, making it harder and slower to block a refinery in court.
The President must designate federal lands — including at least three closed military installations — as potential refinery sites and offer them for lease exclusively for refinery construction.
During a fuel supply emergency after a natural disaster, the President may temporarily waive federal fuel requirements and preempt matching state and local rules for up to 90 days.
Selling gasoline or diesel at 'price gouging' levels in a major disaster area becomes a federal offense with civil penalties, and an FTC investigation into post-Katrina gasoline prices is required.

Qualified small refineries receive rebates of up to $4.50 per barrel on crude oil the government sells from its royalty-in-kind supply, and FERC becomes the lead agency coordinating federal pipeline approvals.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of the standby support account, disaster assistance to energy companies, and grant programs if the bill passes. People living near designated refinery or pipeline sites bear the local air-quality and siting consequences of weakened Clean Air Act requirements, faster permitting, and consolidated court review. States lose leverage: their fuel rules can be preempted in an emergency, stricter state paperwork requirements are targeted for streamlining, and only the FTC (not states) can enforce the price-gouging ban. Drivers see no direct benefit unless new refining capacity actually lowers prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and communities near refinery sites

drawbacks.text: The bill weakens Clean Air Act protections: it targets New Source Review reforms in the introduced version, extends ozone attainment deadlines for downwind areas, lets facilities burn biomass debris without triggering new-source requirements, and lets the President waive fuel controls — including state equivalents — for 90 days in an emergency.

The Standby Refinery Support Account makes taxpayers the insurer of refinery construction: the government pays builders' delay costs, debt interest, and consequential damages if lawsuits or agency delays slow a project.
The price-gouging ban is narrow — it applies only during declared disasters and only the FTC and Attorney General can enforce it, preempting state and local enforcement.

Nothing in the bill requires refiners to pass savings to consumers, and the industry was already running at 95 percent utilization — so the supply gains were uncertain while the environmental and regulatory concessions were definite.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundled a few genuinely consumer-facing items — a disaster-area gouging ban, carpool grants, an expanded Northeast heating oil reserve — with much larger structural concessions to the refining and pipeline industries: federal payment of builders' delay costs, softened air rules, and legal channels that make local opposition harder. Even supporters' own findings section acknowledged households were spending record shares of income on gasoline, but the bill's consumer benefits were indirect and contingent on new capacity being built, while the regulatory relief for industry was immediate and unconditional. As drafted, the trade tilted toward concentrated interests.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House by two votes on a straight party-line vote, then sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee for the rest of the Congress and never got a Senate vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Barton introduced the bill on September 26, 2005, three weeks after Hurricane Katrina hit Gulf Coast refining, and it cleared the House Energy and Commerce Committee by voice vote within two days.
On October 7, 2005, a Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions failed 200-222, with 196 of 202 House Democrats in favor and all but 3 Republicans opposed.
The House then passed the bill 212-210; every one of the 212 yes votes was a Republican, no Democrat voted yes, and 13 Republicans voted no.

The Senate received the bill on October 17, 2005, referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on October 24, and the committee never reported it; the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the Senate never acted, oil refiners and pipeline developers never received the federal delay-cost backstop, the designated federal refinery sites, or the softened Clean Air Act rules; communities near potential sites and state regulators kept the existing legal protections. Consumers also never got the bill's narrow gouging ban, which was folded into the same package.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split entirely by party: all 212 yes votes were Republican, none of the 202 Democrats voted yes, and 13 Republicans joined 196 Democrats and the one Independent in opposition for a two-vote margin.

industries.note: The bill hands refiners federal payment of delay costs (including debt interest), presidentially designated refinery sites, streamlined permitting with court-enforced deadlines, extended ozone deadlines, and presidential authority to waive fuel rules in emergencies. The industry's gain comes partly at the cost of weaker air-pollution controls around refinery communities.

industries.industry: Crude oil and petroleum product pipeline operators
industries.note: FERC becomes lead agency coordinating pipeline approvals with binding deadlines, and challenges go straight to the D.C. Circuit on an expedited basis, reducing the leverage of state agencies and local opponents.
Qualified small refineries get rebates of up to $4.50 per barrel on government royalty oil, a targeted subsidy subject to appropriations.

The bill creates a federal price-gouging offense with civil penalties during declared disasters, but enforcement is exclusive to the FTC and Attorney General, preempting the stricter state-level gouging laws that had been used after Katrina.

Federal loan guarantees for the Alaska natural gas pipeline would sunset unless the state signed a contract binding gas deliveries to the pipeline, pressing the state and producers to commit to the project.
